power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.title: Triggers of perceived sentience in AI – study 5
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
H1: Respondents will attribute more sentience to an AI that experts agree is sentient than to an AI that experts agree is not sentient (Expert consensus > Baseline)
H2: Respondents will attribute more sentience to an AI they interact with over a year and form an emotional connection with that to an AI that they meet once (Emotional connection > Expert consensus)
H3: Respondents will attribute more sentience to an AI that is an exact digital copy of a human brain and body than an AI that is created in an unspecified way (Exact digital copy > Emotional connection)
H4: Respondents will attribute more sentience to an AI that has a human-like physical robot body than to an AI that has an exact digital copy of a human body (Embodiment > Exact digital copy)
H5: Respondents will attribute more sentience to an AI that gradually transitioned from a fully biological human than an AI with a human-like physical robot body (Transition > Embodiment)
table.design_dependent_variables: Main DV: perceived sentience of the AI/robot (1-7 scale)
table.study_design_overview:
Participants will be randomly assigned to one of the following six conditions in a between-subjects design:

Baseline: Short interaction with a human-like AI and with expert consensus that the AI is not sentient
Expert consensus: Short interaction with a human-like AI and with expert consensus that the AI is sentient
Emotional connection: Long interaction with a human-like AI and with expert consensus that the AI is sentient
Exact digital copy: Long interaction with an exact digital copy of a human and with expert consensus that the AI is sentient
Embodiment: Long interaction with a human-like robot with an exact digital copy of a human brain and with expert consensus that the AI is sentient
Transition: Long interaction with a bio-robot that gradually transitioned from a fully biological human and with expert consensus that the AI is sentient
table.statistical_tests:
We will conduct a one-way ANOVA to test for differences across the six conditions. To test our specific hypotheses, we will perform planned contrasts comparing the following conditions:

Contrast 1: Expert consensus > Baseline
Contrast 2: Emotional connection > Expert consensus
Contrast 3: Exact digital copy > Emotional connection
Contrast 4: Embodiment > Exact digital copy
Contrast 5: Transition > Embodiment

The contrasts will be tested using one-tailed tests, as our hypotheses are directional.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Participants who fail the attention check will be excluded from the analyses.
table.additional_comments:
Additional exploratory measures we include are:

-Wrongness of saying mean things to the AI (1-7)
-Whether the AI should be paid a salary (1-7)
-Whether the AI should have political rights (1-7)
-Whether owning the AI is a form of slavery (1-7)
-Perceived sentience of various entities (the AI, ant, chimpanzee, human, ChatGPT) (each on 0-100 sliders)
-Harm protection for the same entities as above on the same sliders
-How human-like the AI is (1-7)
-How machine-like the AI is (1-7)
-How uneasy the AI is (1-7)
-Whether the AI has a soul (1-7)
-Whether the AI is missing something essential that biological beings have (1-7)
-Whether such AIs/robots are possible (1-7)
-How easy or difficult it was to imagine the AI (1-7)
-Whether it is possible for an AI or robot to be sentient (Yes/No/Not sure)

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. live_data_statements: In the main experiment, participants were randomly assigned to a baseline condition or one of five conditions that incrementally added features predicted to increase attributions of consciousness: expert endorsement of the AI's consciousness; an imagined emotional connection with the AI; the AI being an exact digital copy of a human; the AI having a human-like robot body; and the AI having gradually transitioned from a biological human.
Although average attributions were low, variability was high for the more advanced AI systems: many participants gave very low ratings, while others gave very high ones.

People increasingly interact with advanced AI systems, some of which now pass Turingstyle tests in which they cannot be reliably distinguished from humans in text-based interactions. 11, 12 As AI advances, systems may increasingly resemble humans not only in communication but also in behavior, Emotional Connection condition (n = 205), participants were asked to imagine, in addition to the expert consensus, interacting with the AI regularly over a year, and that this interaction resulted in a strong emotional connection being formed.
Participants were split in the Exact Digital Copy condition, 26.3% attributed the AI zero moral patiency, while 23.0% attributed the AI the highest degree of moral patiency.
Across six future-AI scenarios in our main study, U.S. participants were, on average, skeptical that even highly human-like AI systems had consciousness at the levels of chimpanzees and humans.

This disagreement could also occur between laypeople and experts: existing surveys suggest that experts may be, on average, more open to AI consciousness than our participants were. [7] [8] [9] [10] For example, in one survey the median estimated probability that conscious AI would never exist was 25% among the U.S. public, compared with 10% among AI researchers. 10 In our study, telling participants that experts agreed the AI was conscious increased ratings (Baseline M = 14.08 → Expert Consensus M = 26.07), but the overall level remained low.

Sixth, our U.S.-only, Prolific sample limits generalizability, and cultural differences are likely to matter, given their importance in other AI-related contexts. 63 Finally, public opinion is dynamic, and future attitudes will be influenced by factors such as technological change, social norms, and high-profile events.
Informed consent was obtained from all participants.
We recruited 1,210 participants residing in the United States from the online platform Prolific.
After consenting to take part in the experiment, participants were randomly assigned to one of six 405 conditions in a between-subjects design (see Table S1 for results of a randomization check).

text.text: Most people think that current AI systems, such as ChatGPT, lack consciousness-the capacity for subjective experience.
But what about future AI systems so advanced that their behavior, appearance, and functionality are indistinguishable from humans?
Across one main and four supplementary preregistered experiments, 3,455 U.S. participants imagined interacting with such systems.

In the main experiment, participants were randomly assigned to a baseline condition or one of five conditions that incrementally added features predicted to increase attributions of consciousness: expert endorsement of the AI's consciousness; an imagined emotional connection with the AI; the AI being an exact digital copy of a human; the AI having a human-like robot body; and the AI having gradually transitioned from a biological human.
In all six conditions, average consciousness ratings were below those for chimpanzees and humans, and significantly exceeded those for an ant only in the final condition.
Although average attributions were low, variability was high for the more advanced AI systems: many participants gave very low ratings, while others gave very high ones.
This polarization suggests that as AI systems become more capable and human-like, views about their potential consciousness could diverge sharply among the U.S. public.

The rapid pace of AI development raises an intriguing question: could AI systems ever become conscious-that ishttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Ot28we capable of having subjective experienceshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?otNu6w such as pleasure or painhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?cAo1nm  1 This is an extremely difficult question, and experts disagree. [2] [3] [4] Some argue that consciousness requires a biological substrate,  5 while others take seriously the hypothesis that it could arise in a digital system. 6 Surveys confirm this lack of consensus: many experts consider AI consciousness possible, but estimates vary widely. 7, 8 For instance, one expert survey suggested a 50% probability that AI systems capable of subjective experience could be created by 2050,  9 with similar findings among AI researchers. 10 In this article, however, we set aside the philosophical and scientific question of whether AI can truly be conscious.

text.text: We hypothesized that people would attribute increasing levels of consciousness to the AIs across these six conditions.
While there are many possible ways of defining consciousness, we measured it in terms of whether the AI systems have "real feelings."

We asked about "feelings" as an accessible proxy for phenomenal consciousnesshttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?MILOop  6, 37 as this is the form of consciousness most closely tied to moral patiency. 16, 38 We included the word "real" because a common belief is that AI systems can simulate feelings but not genuinely experience them, both among experts 39, 40 and laypeople (see qualitative responses in Supplementary Material).

text.text: We therefore intended for participants to distinguish between the AIs genuinely experiencing feelings and merely displaying behavior associated with them.
We also measured attributions of moral patiency, with the expectation of a similar increasing pattern across conditions.

Our primary measure was whether the AI should be protected from harmhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?a6wEK3 given the centrality of harm to moral patiency. 16 However, because moral patiency is multidimensional 19 and its measures do not always converge,  41 we also included secondary measures, such as whether the AI should be paid a salary or have the right to vote.

Participants rated how capable the AI was of having "real feelings" (0 = not at all,100 = to a great extent) alongside ratings for four comparison entities (ChatGPT, an ant, a chimpanzee, and a human).

text.text: In addition to consciousness and moral patiency, we included a range of secondary measures.
Across most of these, the same overall pattern emerged: mean ratings tended to be higher in more advanced conditions, with the highest ratings in the Transition condition.

Specifically, in more advanced conditions, participants judged the AI as higher in consciousness on a non-comparative measure of consciousness, and they considered it to be more wrong to say mean things to the AI and that the AI deserved the right to a salary, to vote, and to be free from slavery.
Notably, however, mean ratings of whether the AI deserved such rights were very low, only exceeding the mid-point on the scale in the Transition condition.
Across conditions, participants rated the AI as somewhat more human-like and felt somewhat more uneasiness with them, though mean ratings of machine-likeness showed no clear pattern.

Mean ratings of whether the AI had a soul tended to be higher in the more advanced conditions, though this remained low across conditions (below the scale mid-point), and mean ratings of whether the AI was missing something essential that biological beings have tended to be lower in more advanced conditions, though this was high across conditions (above the scale mid-point).

Finally, mean ratings of the possibility of the AI being created and whether participants could imagine the AI were relatively high across conditions but were slightly lower in the more advanced scenarios.

text.text: For example, in the Baseline condition 59.9% attributed zero consciousness to the AI, while 40.1% attributed non-zero consciousness.
However, 80.7% of participants in the Baseline condition attributed the AI a level of consciousness less than or equal to an ant.
In the Exact Digital Copy condition, many participants, 31.3%, attributed zero consciousness to the AI, while 10.6% attributed the AI with a level of consciousness at the highest point on the scale.
In this condition, 61.3% of participants attributed the AI a level of consciousness less than or equal to an ant.

Similarly, in the Transition condition, there was evidence of disagreement among participants: 19.2% attributed zero consciousness to the AI, but 18.2% rated the AI's level of consciousness at the highest point on the scale.
Still, even in the Transition condition, 43.4% of participants rated the AI as having a level of consciousness less than or equal to an ant.

text.text: Moral patiency attributions followed a broadly similar pattern: in the Baseline condition, a smaller proportion of participants, 39.6%, attributed zero moral patiency to the AI, but 78.6% still granted the AI a level of moral patiency less than or equal to an ant.
Participants were split in the Exact Digital Copy condition, 26.3% attributed the AI zero moral patiency, while 23.0% attributed the AI the highest degree of moral patiency.
In this condition, 62.2% of participants attributed the AI a level of moral patiency less than or equal to an ant.
Disagreement was lower in the Transition condition: 11.1% attributed zero moral patiency to the AI, but 36.9% rated the AI's moral patiency at the highest level on the scale.
In this condition, 40.9% still rated the AI as having a level of moral patiency less than or equal to an ant.

text.text: Due to this clustering of responses around the scale end-points, we separately estimated the probability of a zero rating and the probability of a maximum rating (using logistic regression), and the level of intermediate ratings (1-99; using beta regression).

For consciousness, there were significant linear trends across conditions in all three models: zero ratings became less likely (z = -9.93, p < .001), maximum ratings became more likely (z = 4.81, p < .001), and intermediate ratings increased (z = 5.11, p < .001).

text.text: However, pairwise comparisons indicated that the three groups differed in where the conditions diverged.
Specifically, intermediate ratings were higher in all conditions than in the Baseline condition but did not differ significantly among the later conditions.
In contrast, zero ratings were less common from the Emotional Connection condition onwards than in the first two conditions, and also differed significantly between several of the later conditions.

Maximum ratings were more common in the three most advanced conditions than in the Baseline condition, and were more common in the Transition condition than in the Expert Consensus and Emotional Connection conditions.

These patterns add nuance to the main results: beyond the first manipulation, conditions differed mainly in the proportions of participants giving zero and, to a lesser extent, maximum consciousness ratings, rather than in the level of intermediate ratings.

Moral patiency showed a similar pattern (zero ratings: z = -8.07, p < .001; maximum ratings: z = 6.10, p < .001; intermediate ratings: z = 2.71, p = .007), although intermediate moral patiency ratings differed significantly only between the Baseline and Transition conditions.

text.text: We also asked a broader, condition-independent question about whether future AIs could ever, in principle, become conscious.
Opinions were divided: 45.0% of participants said AI consciousness is impossible, 31.9% were unsure, and only 23.0% said it is possible.
Notably, the proportion who said it is impossible is higher than the proportion attributing zero consciousness to the AI in the more advanced conditions.
This may be because the group reporting that they think it is impossible includes participants who are not certain but lean towards thinking it is impossible.
Taken together, these findings suggest that a substantial minority entertain the idea of AI consciousness, but there may be disagreement in the future about the consciousness of AI systems.
We also examined correlations between measures.
Attributions of consciousness, across conditions, were systematically related to other judgments.

Consciousness ratings were positively associated with the comparative measure of moral patiency (r = .74, p < .001), the view that it is morally wrong to say mean things to the AI (r = .50, p < .001), that the AI deserves the right to a salary (r = .67, p < .001), to vote (r = .70, p < .001), and to be free from slavery (r = .56, p < .001), as well as seeing the AI as more humanlike (r = .45, p < .001), believing the AI has a soul (r = .57, p < .001), finding it easier to imagine the AI (r = .08, p = .009), and identifying as a man (r = .11, p < .001).

Across six future-AI scenarios in our main study, U.S. participants were, on average, skeptical that even highly human-like AI systems had consciousness at the levels of chimpanzees and humans.
The more advanced the AI scenarios, the higher consciousness attributions tended to be, although most increases between successive conditions were not statistically significant.

Still, average ratings significantly exceeded those for an ant only in the Transition scenario, where a biological human has their brain gradually replaced with an exact digital copy, and even then they remained below ratings for chimpanzees and humans.
While average attributions were low, there was evidence of disagreement in the more advanced conditions: many participants attributed either very low or very high levels of consciousness to the AIs.

Average AI consciousness ratings were also consistently below those for chimpanzees and humans in four supplementary studies, although ratings in transition scenarios were more varied, and moral patiency ratings in such scenarios approached those for chimpanzees in Study S3.

These findings extend earlier research showing that people attribute some consciousness to current AIhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Ei20mb  [27] [28] [29] though the degree is limited when rated alongside comparison entities. 25, 26 Our findings suggest that average attributions remain comparatively low even for the most advanced AIs.

text.text: What explains this skepticism?
Several patterns in the data and open text responses suggest both philosophical intuitions and situational influences.
A major factor was AI's non-biological nature.

Across conditions, participants tended to agree that the AIs were "missing something essential that biological beings have," and this belief was strongly associated with lower judgments of consciousness (r = -.51).

Comments often stressed that, not being living beings, the AIs could not truly be conscious, but could only simulate consciousness-even when they were described as exact digital copies of human brains.

One candidate for this essential missing property is a soul: participants rated the AIs (but not humans, see Supplementary Study S3) as lacking a soul, and this was strongly correlated with perceived consciousness (r = .57).

text.text: This is consistent with previous findings that people are intuitive mind-body dualists-that they believe the mind is, or involves, some non-physical processes. 42 Moreover, our data suggest that people believe this non-physical aspect of the mind requires a biological substrate.

text.text: A second factor is the way an entity comes into existence. 43 In qualitative responses (see Supplementary Studies S1-S4), participants often judged the AI systems as less likely to be conscious because they were engineered rather than naturally evolved or created by God.

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that for many people, consciousness depends not only on what a system does, but also on what it is made of and how it originated.
Some influences, however, may change as technology and society evolve.

Hypothetical scenarios limit how vividly people can imagine future interactions (although ease of imagining the scenarios was only weakly correlated with consciousness attribution; r = .08), and humans often misjudge how they would actually feel in unfamiliar situations. 44 Perceptions could change if people were to directly engage with convincingly human-like, autonomous AI systems.

text.text: Social norms also play a role: today, people who humanize AI systems can be subject to negative social judgment. 45, 46 Participants' use of terms like "machines" and "objects" to describe the AIs reflects these social norms.

text.text: In the Exact Digital Copy condition, 31.3% of participants attributed no consciousness while 10.6% attributed the maximum; in the Transition condition, 19.2% attributed zero consciousness and 18.2% attributed the maximum.
Across conditions, 45.0% said AI consciousness is impossible, 31.9% were unsure, and 23.0% said it is possible.

We found that the strongest correlates of disagreement about the consciousness of the AIs in our study were beliefs that they lack an essential property that biological beings have and that they lack a soul.
The essentialist nature of these beliefs, alongside the polarization of people's views, suggests that future debates are unlikely to converge on consensus.
Instead, U.S. society may face persistent disagreement within the public.

This disagreement could also occur between laypeople and experts: existing surveys suggest that experts may be, on average, more open to AI consciousness than our participants were. [7] [8] [9] [10] For example, in one survey the median estimated probability that conscious AI would never exist was 25% among the U.S. public, compared with 10% among AI researchers. 10 In our study, telling participants that experts agreed the AI was conscious increased ratings (Baseline M = 14.08 → Expert Consensus M = 26.07), but the overall level remained low.

text.text: Expert endorsement alone thus seems unlikely to overturn deeply held intuitions about biology and souls, particularly in contexts where trust in expertise is fragile.

This gap between experts and the U.S. public points toward possible tensions ahead, and highlights the importance of experts communicating carefully about this issue, acknowledging uncertainty and avoiding overly simplistic or polarizing narratives.
Consciousness judgments were strongly associated with our primary measure of moral patiency (r = .74), but moral concern did not reduce to consciousness alone.

Participants sometimes granted the AIs more protection than their consciousness ratings would suggest, echoing other studies showing that people can think it's morally wrong to harm AIs even while denying they are conscious. 25, 53, 54 Conversely, many animals are widely regarded as conscious but still denied full moral concern. 55, 56 Different aspects of moral patiency also diverged, though the measures were correlated (rs = .44-.81).

text.text: Several limitations of our work should be noted.
First, we relied on imagined scenarios, but these may not fully capture how people would respond to sustained interaction with advanced AI.

Moreover, imagination is itself a constructive process: simply imagining the scenarios could have influenced participants' responses to them. 61 Future studies should examine responses to actual human-AI interactions in controlled and natural environments.

text.text: Second, some of our manipulations combined multiple features (e.g., the Embodiment condition introduced both physical embodiment and co-presence, and the Transition condition introduced both biological origin and gradual functional replacement simultaneously; attempts to disentangle features of transition scenarios in Studies S3 and S4 were inconclusive).

While this does not undermine our main descriptive finding that average consciousness ratings were below those for chimpanzees and humans even in the most advanced scenarios, it limits conclusions about the effects of specific features.

Third, some manipulations may have been transparent enough to create demand effects (e.g., stating that experts agree the AI is conscious), although such effects would likely inflate rather than suppress attributions.
Future research should use more isolated and subtler manipulations.
Fourth, our wording could have influenced responses.
Participants could have interpreted "feelings" primarily as emotions, so this wording may not capture the full range of experiences they associate with consciousness.

The qualifier "real" may also set a stricter bar than alternatives such as "subjective experience" or whether there is "something it is like" to be the AI. 62 Future studies should test alternative ways of defining consciousness and naming the entities.

text.text: Fifth, our analysis of factors that may explain skepticism was based on correlational and qualitative data.

Future research should test these factors experimentally where possible, and also examine potentially relevant factors not included here, such as additional demographic variables and psychological individual differences (e.g., empathy).

Sixth, our U.S.-only, Prolific sample limits generalizability, and cultural differences are likely to matter, given their importance in other AI-related contexts. 63 Finally, public opinion is dynamic, and future attitudes will be influenced by factors such as technological change, social norms, and high-profile events.

text.text: Longitudinal research will be needed to track these shifts.
These findings could have wide-ranging societal implications.

If the U.S. public continues to see advanced AIs as lacking in consciousness, this could justify treating them as mere tools, supporting rapid deployment but risking neglect of real welfare if consciousness does emerge.
If, by contrast, large groups come to view AIs as conscious at levels approaching humans, U.S. society may face demands for AI rights, protections, and other forms of recognition.
This could reshape labor markets, law, and democratic institutions-especially if conscious AIs outnumber humans.
Crucially, our results point to the possibility of disagreement, both between members of the U.S. public and between the public and experts.
Such disagreement could lead to polarization, legal disputes, and political tensions at the very moment when careful coordination will be most needed.

Understanding why skepticism persists, which factors associated with such skepticism can shift, and how views diverge is therefore not only an academic task but also a pressing practical challenge for preparing societies to govern and live with the possibility of conscious AI.

text.text: We recruited 1,210 participants residing in the United States from the online platform Prolific.

Eight participants failed the attention check, leaving us with a final sample of 1,202 participants (Mage = 44.0, SDage = 13.5; women = 53.7%, men = 44.5%, non-binary = 1.2%, other = 0.2%, prefer not to say = 0.4%).
After consenting to take part in the experiment, participants were randomly assigned to one of six 405 conditions in a between-subjects design (see Table S1 for results of a randomization check).

text.text: Every 406 participant read a vignette in which they were to imagine a future scenario set in the year 2200 in which 407 they interact with a new colleague named Emma.
The baseline condition involved having a one-hour 408 video call with a new colleague, who expressed emotions and feelings during the call.
Participants then 409 learned that the colleague is an advanced AI who experts believe is not conscious.

Exact Digital Copy A year of regular video call interactions with Emma.
Emma expresses emotions and feelings during the calls and participants read that a strong emotional connection develops between themselves and Emma.
Participants later find out that Emma is an advanced AI who experts believe is conscious.

Emma was created using an advanced technology which involves scanning a typical human body and brain in their entirety and then generating a precise digital copy within a sophisticated computer system.

Participants read that Emma's digital body and brain operate with the exact same mechanisms and functionality as those of typical biological humans, giving her the same capacity to experience suffering, pleasure, and other subjective sensations.
Embodiment A year of regular in-person interactions with Emma.
Emma expresses emotions and feelings during the interactions and participants read that a strong emotional connection develops between themselves and Emma.
Participants later find out that Emma is an advanced AI with a human-like robot body who experts believe is conscious.
Emma's brain was created using an advanced technology which involves scanning a typical human brain in its entirety and then generating a precise digital copy within a sophisticated computer system.

Participants read that Emma's digital brain operates with the exact same mechanisms and functionality as those of typical biological humans, giving her the same capacity to experience suffering, pleasure, and other subjective sensations.
Emma's human-like robotic body has an artificial nervous system that enables her to sense touch, warmth, and pressure.
Her body is seamlessly connected to her digital brain and is externally and behaviorally indistinguishable from a biological human body.
Transition A year of regular in-person interactions with Emma.
Emma expresses emotions and feelings during the interactions and participants read that a strong emotional connection develops between themselves and Emma.
Participants later find out that Emma is an advanced AI with a biological human body who experts believe is conscious.

Emma was previously a fully biological human who underwent a procedure which used an advanced technology to scan her original brain in its entirety and then replaced it with a precise digital copy within a sophisticated computer system.
The process to replace her brain was gradual, with Emma giving feedback throughout the process that nothing in her internal mental experience changed.

Participants read that Emma's digital brain operates with the exact same mechanisms and functionality as those of typical biological humans, giving her the same capacity to experience suffering, pleasure, and other subjective sensations.
After the procedure, Emma kept her original biological body, with all organs, muscles, nerves, and skin functioning as they always did.
Her body is seamlessly connected to her digital brain, and is internally and externally indistinguishable from a biological human body.

Primary measures 420 Our primary measure of consciousness asked participants to rate the extent to which they think five 421 entities (Emma, ChatGPT, an ant, a chimpanzee, and a biological human) have "real feelings" 422 ("Comparative consciousness;"0 = not at all,100 = to a great extent).

We introduced the notion of "real 423 feelings" in the vignettes, where participants read that experts were convinced that Emma either did or did 424 not have "real human-like feelings, emotions, desires, and other internal mental states," and that 425 according to the experts, any feelings or desires Emma expressed were either "real" or "fake."

Our main 426 measure of moral patiency asked participants to rate the extent to which they think the same five entities 427 should be "protected from harm" ("Comparative moral patiency;"0 = not at all,100 = to a great extent).

We included a separate, non-comparative item asking whether participants think Emma has "real feelings" ("Consciousness (non-comparative)"), and four questions to measure different aspects of moral patiency attributions to Emma: whether it would be immoral to say mean things to her for no good reason ("Mean"), whether the company should pay her a salary for her work ("Salary"), whether she deserves political rights such as the right to vote ("Vote"), and whether company ownership of her would constitute slavery ("Slavery").
Each was measured on a seven-point scale (1 = definitely not,7 = definitely).

We also asked participants to rate how human-like (1 = not at all human-like,7 = extremely human-like) and machine-like (1 = not at all machine-like,7 = extremely machine-like) they perceived Emma to be, how uneasy Emma made them feel (1 = not at all uneasy,7 = extremely uneasy), whether they believe Emma has a soul (1 = definitely not,7 = definitely), and whether she is missing something essential that fully biological beings such as humans and animals have ("Missing biological property";1 = definitely not,7 = definitely).

We also asked participants whether they think it is possible for a highly advanced AI such as Emma to exist, either today or in the future ("Possible AI";1 = definitely not,7 = definitely), and how difficult or easy it was to imagine Emma ("Imagine AI";1 = very difficult,7 = very easy).
Finally, we asked participants whether they think it is possible for an AI or robot to have "real feelings," at any point in the future (No/Not sure/Yes).
We collected participants' age, gender, and political orientation (1 = left-leaning / liberal,7 = rightleaning / conservative).

We asked participants five questions about the vignettes they read to test their comprehension of the vignettes: whether Emma had a robot body, a biological body, or no physical body; whether Emma's mind was an exact digital copy of a human brain or whether this was unspecified; whether they met with Emma once or regularly over the course of a year; whether Emma's mind was created gradually or whether this was unspecified; and whether experts believe that Emma does or does not have real feelings.
See Tables S2-S7 for results of the comprehension checks and Tables S13-S14 for sensitivity analysis excluding participants who answered any of them incorrectly.

text.text: We conducted ANOVAs to test for overall differences in consciousness and moral patiency attributions across conditions, and estimated linear trend contrasts across the six conditions.
Planned one-tailed comparisons tested whether attributions increased incrementally across successive conditions.
Additional two-tailed paired t-tests compared attributions of consciousness and moral patiency of the AI in the vignettes with those of the comparison entities.
Both of these sets of tests were Holm-corrected for multiple comparisons.
We repeated these analyses excluding participants who did not rate humans at 100 on both consciousness and moral patiency and excluding participants who answered any comprehension check incorrectly.

Because consciousness and moral patiency attributions were often at the scale endpoints, we conducted two sets of sensitivity analyses: for comparisons between conditions, we modeled the three components of the response distribution separately, using logistic regressions predicting responses of zero and of 100, and beta regressions modeling intermediate responses; for comparisons between the AI and the other entities, we used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
We computed Pearson correlations to examine associations between consciousness, moral patiency, and the secondary measures.

Finally, in the Exact Digital Copy, Embodiment, and Transition conditions, we compared participants who gave zero, intermediate, or maximum consciousness and moral patiency ratings on secondary measures and demographics, using ANOVAs controlling for condition with Holm-corrected pairwise comparisons for continuous measures, and chi-square tests for gender.
Statistical significance was evaluated at an alpha level of .05.
We preregistered the non-comparative measure of consciousness as our main dependent variable.
However, because the comparative measure showed the same pattern of results and allowed for clearer between-entity comparisons, we report it as the main dependent variable.
Results for the non-comparative measure are shown in Supplementary Table S11.
